The papersThe code

MA-Networker, dug back up.

21 results: 1 exact, 4 agree, 7 partly agree, 1 inconclusive, 5 differ, 3 not attempted. MA-Networker was never released, so it was rebuilt from the paper and run on the same ChIP data and an expression library rebuilt from the SGD archive.

Gao et al. 2004BMC Bioinformatics 5:31 Defining transcriptional networks Fig. 1DiffersTable 1Partly agreesFig. 2Partly agreesTable 3Partly agreesFig. 3Partly agreesMain claimDiffers In the overlay, ink is theirs and green is ours

Fig. 1

Fig. 1. (b) Activity profiles of Hap4, Ndd1 and Ste12 over stress (red), pheromone (green) and cell cycle (blue) experiments. (c) ChIP binding log ratio against coupling for the same TFs: B- black, B+/C+ red, B+/C- green. Panel a is a diagram.

Differs
Fig. 1b, activity profiles of Hap4, Ndd1 and Ste12
3 of 3 values, Agrees
Fig. 1c, Hap4 binding against coupling
52.5% within 2 px, Partly agrees
Fig. 1c, Ndd1 binding against coupling
59.0% within 2 px, Inconclusive
Fig. 1c, Ste12 binding against coupling
27.5% within 2 px, Differs

Our B+/C+ (red) and B+/C- (green) points fall in the published places better than any control, but our couplings are larger in magnitude (r from -0.81 to 0.92; B+/C+ genes up to 0.71, against about 0.65 in the paper), so many of our points sit above the published ones. The rebuilt library (2010 reprocessing, 677 arrays) is the likely reason; it cannot be checked without the authors' 2003 library or coupling_result. Our coupling scaled by 0.9 scores better than ours, so the score cannot confirm our coupling scale for Ndd1: our couplings are larger in magnitude than the published ones, as for Hap4, although the split itself is close (50 B+/C+ and 44 B+/C- against 50 and 42). Our Ste12 couplings are much stronger than the published ones (our B+/C+ genes reach r 0.67; the paper's stop near 0.45), and we call 25 B+/C+ and 25 B+/C- against 19 and 31. Our pheromone experiments are 15 Roberts 2000 arrays, where the paper had 56; Ste12's activity is carried by them.

Both scores above 12 come back, and every regulatory call of the figure is the same (RAD51, RPL40B, FSP2 and HXT9 coupled; PUP3 and MLP1 not), but the other printed scores differ (Mbp1 to RAD51 11.1 against 8.7), as our couplings are stronger throughout (see fig1c). Hap6 cannot be computed: it is not in the ChIP data.

Table 2, deletion responseNot attemptedThe text says Table 2 averages Hughes et al.'s mutant/wild-type log ratios, but its genome-wide means (0.52 to 0.83, SD 0.12 to 0.34) are not log ratios: the genome-wide mean of the log10 ratios is 0.00 (SD 0.05 to 0.17) and of their absolute values 0.03 to 0.11. The values fit Hughes et al.'s per-gene P-values, which are not public (the Rosetta download sits behind a registration form; the SGD file has ratios only). The claim the table supports is checked from the ratios as text.deletion.

Python package manetworker and its tutorialAgrees

The main claim nearly comes back: 59% of bound genes couple in our run, against the paper's 58%. The validations point the same way as the paper's. The numbers differ because the expression library was rebuilt (677 of 751 arrays, reprocessed in 2010), because GO and motif settings are not stated, and because Hughes et al.'s P-values, behind Table 2 and Table 4, are not public.

What came back

The method
MA-Networker as the Python package manetworker: regression, backward selection, coupling and the false discovery rate, from the paper's Methods.
Fig. 1b
Hap4 moves most in stress, Ndd1 in the cell cycle, Ste12 with pheromone, as the caption says.
Table 1
Bound genes per TF within 8 of the paper's for every TF; 59% of them couple against 58%.
Divergent promoters
1592 of 4532 ChIP probes shared by two genes, exactly as printed.
Fig. 2
The vector bars read exactly from the paper's own file; most B+/C- groups have no enriched GO category, as in the paper.
Fig. 3
Every coupling call of the figure is the same; both scores above 12 come back.

What stayed buried

  • The authors' 751-array library: 74 arrays are not in the SGD archive, and the rest were reprocessed in 2010.
  • The authors' released activity and coupling files: their site refuses scripted downloads and the web archive was out of reach from this run.
  • Table 2 and Table 4: they rest on Hughes et al.'s per-gene P-values, which sit behind a registration form. Table 2's numbers are those P-values, not the log ratios the text names.
  • Hap6 in Fig. 3: it is not among the 113 TFs of the ChIP data.

The main claim nearly comes back: 59% of bound genes couple in our run, against the paper's 58%. The validations point the same way as the paper's. The numbers differ because the expression library was rebuilt (677 of 751 arrays, reprocessed in 2010), because GO and motif settings are not stated, and because Hughes et al.'s P-values, behind Table 2 and Table 4, are not public.

What we matched

How each part of the paper's method was rebuilt.

ChIP data
Lee et al. 2002, 113 TFs, the file the paper used; bound means P below 0.001.
Expression
677 arrays from 15 of the paper's 19 sources, from the SGD archive, as log2 ratios.
Step 1
A regression per array on all TFs; backward selection at P = 0.005/751.
Step 2
Pearson correlation of each gene with each activity profile; 5% false discovery rate.
Validation
GO release 2004-03 (the oldest archived), Hughes 2000 deletions, the S288C genome, Simon et al. 2001 ChIP.

MA-Networker came back from the paper's text; its 2003 expression library did not.
